analysis.one_liner: Bans corporations that hire registered lobbyists from spending on election ads.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up: it sat in the House Administration Committee with no cosponsors until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal campaign finance law to say that any corporation that employs or retains a registered lobbyist cannot spend money on independent political expenditures or 'electioneering communications' — the ads run before elections that praise or attack candidates without coordinating with their campaigns. The idea is that a corporation should not be able to both lobby Congress behind the scenes and spend corporate money to influence who gets elected. It was introduced by one representative and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who worry that corporate-funded campaign ads tilt elections toward the interests of lobbying firms and the companies that hire them. The bill's findings argue that corporate independent spending creates corruption or the appearance of it, and that the ban would restore public confidence in elections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates facing corporate ad spending

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a corporation from making any expenditure, or any disbursement for an electioneering communication, if it employs or retains a registered lobbyist under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995.
The bill's stated rationale is that independent expenditures by corporations give rise to corruption and the appearance of corruption, and threaten public faith in democracy.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that hire registered lobbyists — large companies in regulated industries would lose the ability to use corporate treasury money for campaign ads while lobbying for their interests, though they could still fund ads through PACs or affiliates that do not lobby, or drop lobbying entirely.

drawbacks.text: The restriction applies only to corporations that employ or retain registered lobbyists; a company could end its lobbying registration and resume campaign spending, or route spending through an affiliate or PAC that does not lobby — so the ban could be engineered around rather than eliminated.
It limits political spending that the Supreme Court's Citizens United line of cases has treated as protected speech, so it would likely face a serious constitutional challenge if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real overlap — the same corporate interests lobby lawmakers and fund campaign ads about them — but the design is narrow and easy to route around, since any company could restructure its lobbying or its ad spending to fit the exception. As a practical policy its effect would be modest; as a statement of principle it went nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee, and nothing else ever happened to it; the Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill on March 13, 2013.
It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and no further action was ever recorded.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with the bill still parked in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that employ lobbyists keep the current rules, in which they can both lobby Congress and spend corporate money on election-season ads; nothing was lost by anyone else, since the bill never had the support to advance.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed a ban on corporate election spending by companies that hire lobbyists.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: The bill would strip these companies of the right to spend corporate treasury money on independent expenditures and electioneering communications while their lobbyists are on the payroll. Its premise is that the same firms shaping legislation behind closed doors should not also buy election ads; the industry's interest in keeping that power runs against the transparency the bill sought.

Corporate clients would face a new cost to retaining a registered lobbyist, since doing so would forfeit campaign spending privileges. Clients might cut back on lobbying or restructure it, shrinking demand for registered lobbying services.

A subset of election-season advertising revenue — corporate-funded ads from companies that lobby — would disappear if the bill took effect, while advertising from companies that do not lobby would be unaffected. The overall effect on the ad industry depends on how large that subset is.
